statement: In children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) and adults with ADHD in double-blind randomized trials of prescribed medicines, analysed at the time closest to 12 weeks (in the blood-pressure review the trials lasted a median of 7 weeks), amphetamine medicines compared with methylphenidate were associated with a slightly larger reduction in clinician-rated ADHD symptoms, a difference the review itself rates as low certainty and that rests partly on indirect comparisons in children and adolescents and only on indirect comparisons in adults, while stopping a trial because of side effects and the rises in blood pressure and pulse did not differ significantly between the two, without being shown to be equal (Cortese et al., 2018; Farhat et al., 2025). The one blinded trial here that gave children both drugs found about the same number of side-effect complaints on each but rated them somewhat more severe on dexamphetamine, at one fixed dose of each and with no placebo (Efron et al., 1997). Benefit: in a network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind trials to April 2017 (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults and 1 in both; 14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults; symptom analyses in 10,068 and 8131), both medicines reduced clinician-rated core symptoms more than placebo, amphetamines by a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 1.02 in children and adolescents and 0.79 in adults and methylphenidate by 0.78 and 0.49 (all four of moderate certainty by the review's GRADE ratings); amphetamines against methylphenidate gave SMDs of −0.24 (95% CI −0.44 to −0.05) in children and adolescents and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05) in adults, both of low certainty, an advantage the authors call marginal in children and adolescents. Teachers' ratings were available for methylphenidate (SMD −0.82 against placebo, low certainty) but not for amphetamines, and clinicians' global improvement ratings did not differ significantly between the two (no estimate printed). The abstract calls the symptom differences head-to-head comparisons, but they are network estimates: by the authors' account head-to-head trials were few and comparisons between drugs were frequently based on indirect evidence, and the network plot shows no trial comparing the two in adults. Stopping because of side effects (11,018 children and adolescents and 5362 adults): against placebo, the odds of leaving a trial because of side effects were higher with amphetamines (odds ratio 2.30, 1.36 to 3.89, in children and adolescents; 3.26, 1.54 to 6.92, in adults; moderate certainty) and with methylphenidate in adults (2.39, 1.40 to 4.08, high certainty), but not clearly with methylphenidate in children and adolescents (1.44, 0.90 to 2.31, low certainty); amphetamines against methylphenidate gave 1.60 (0.94 to 2.73, low certainty) in children and adolescents and 1.36 (0.54 to 3.43, very low certainty) in adults, neither significant, so more stopping on amphetamines is neither shown nor ruled out. The article gives odds ratios only, not how many people stopped. The authors' preference for methylphenidate in children and adolescents and amphetamines in adults rests on each drug's comparison with placebo (in children and adolescents methylphenidate was the only medicine with better acceptability than placebo and, unlike amphetamines, was not worse tolerated than placebo), not on a difference between the two. Both lowered weight against placebo (SMDs −0.71 in children and adolescents and −0.60 in adults with amphetamines, −0.77 and −0.74 with methylphenidate; no comparison of the two is printed). Blood pressure and pulse: in a second network meta-analysis by an overlapping team that reused and extended the first one's searches to January 2024 (102 trials; 13,315 children and adolescents, mean age 11, and 9387 adults, mean age 35; median trial length 7 weeks; 87 of the 102 trials industry funded), the average rises against placebo, which the authors describe as small on average, were: in children and adolescents, systolic pressure +1.81 mm Hg, diastolic +2.42 and pulse +3.88 beats a minute with methylphenidate; +0.87 (not significant), +1.93 and +1.78 (not significant) with amphetamines; and +1.76, +2.29 and +4.17 with lisdexamfetamine, analysed separately; in adults, all of very low certainty, +1.66, +1.6 and +4.37 with methylphenidate, +2.3, +1.91 and +5.18 with amphetamines, and +1.62 (not significant), +3.07 and +5.07 with lisdexamfetamine. Neither amphetamines nor lisdexamfetamine differed significantly from methylphenidate in either age group: amphetamines minus methylphenidate, systolic −0.94 mm Hg (−2.33 to 0.44, high certainty) in children and adolescents and +0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults, diastolic −0.49 (−1.87 to 0.88) and +0.31 (−1.87 to 2.49) (editors' sign reversal of the printed methylphenidate-minus-amphetamines values), and pulse −2.1 beats a minute (−4.25 to 0.06) and +0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90). All adult trials were placebo-controlled, so every adult comparison between medicines is indirect; restricted to licensed doses, the authors report that only amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine were still consistently associated with higher blood pressure than placebo in adults (numbers only in the appendix, not read); only four trials gave 24-week results and none longer; and these are group averages, which the authors say some people may exceed. The head-to-head trial: 125 children aged 5 to 15 (114 boys) referred to a hospital clinic in Melbourne took dexamphetamine, an amphetamine, and methylphenidate in identical capsules twice a day for two weeks each, in random order, with investigators, families, children and teachers blind to the order. On parents' ratings of 17 listed complaints (0 absent, 1 to 9 for severity; a scale without published norms), the mean number of complaints was 7.64 on dexamphetamine and 7.19 on methylphenidate (not different) against 8.19 before treatment, and the mean severity of the complaints reported was 3.73 against 3.24 (significant; 4.08 before treatment); six items were rated more severe on dexamphetamine (trouble sleeping 3.61 against 2.69, irritability 3.65 against 2.94, proneness to crying 3.4 against 2.7, anxiousness 2.71 against 2.07, sadness or unhappiness 2.43 against 1.69, nightmares 0.79 against 0.48), none on methylphenidate, and two children stopped on each drug because of severe effects. Many complaints were already reported before any medicine (irritability in 102 of the 125 children, anxiousness in 96), and only poor appetite (43 before, 74 on dexamphetamine, 69 on methylphenidate) and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine (67 before, 88) were more frequent on a drug than before; with no placebo, changes from before treatment cannot be attributed to the drugs. Each drug was given at one fixed dose set by body weight, and the paper does not report whether the two doses worked equally well (parents rated 86 children improved on dexamphetamine and 90 on methylphenidate, not tested), so the difference in severity may reflect the doses chosen. These are prescribed medicines at licensed or guideline doses, studied over weeks in people diagnosed with ADHD; the papers say nothing about long-term use or about use without a prescription. Psychosis, which neither review studied, is a separate answer (see the answer on psychosis after starting amphetamine or methylphenidate). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Adderall or Ritalin: which works better, and which has more side effects? In reviews of short trials in people with ADHD, both amphetamine medicines (such as Adderall) and methylphenidate (such as Ritalin) eased symptoms clearly more than a dummy pill. On doctors' ratings amphetamine came out slightly ahead, but the review rated that difference low certainty: few trials compared the two directly, none in adults, so the comparison mostly runs through trials against a dummy pill. People did not clearly stop a trial because of side effects more often on one than on the other, though a difference could not be ruled out; compared with a dummy pill, more stopped on amphetamine at every age, and on methylphenidate in adults. Both lowered weight. Over about 7 weeks, blood pressure rose by about 1 to 3 points (mm Hg) and pulse by about 2 to 5 beats a minute on average compared with a dummy pill, with no clear difference between the two medicines. In the one blinded trial that gave 125 children both medicines, two weeks each and with no dummy pill, parents reported about as many complaints on each, but rated sleep and mood complaints (trouble sleeping, irritability, crying, anxiousness, sadness, nightmares) a little more severe on dexamphetamine, a kind of amphetamine; many of these complaints were already there before any medicine. The trials lasted weeks, not years, and they say nothing about taking these medicines without a prescription.

evidence.extracted: Randomized, double-blind crossover trial with no placebo: 125 children (114 boys, 11 girls) aged 5 to 15 with DSM-IV ADHD, referred to a hospital clinic in Melbourne and enrolled from April 1995 to August 1996, took dexamphetamine and methylphenidate as crushed powder in identical capsules, twice a day for 2 weeks each in random order with a 24-hour washout, at one fixed weight-based dose of each (study conditions: 0.15 mg/kg per dose of dexamphetamine, 0.3 mg/kg per dose of methylphenidate); investigators, families, children and teachers were blind to the order. risk_of_bias.note: Network meta-analysis: only 23.5% (children and adolescents) and 27.5% (adults) of the trials were at overall low risk of bias, most unclear; analyses restricted to low-risk trials or by sponsorship could not be done; the article reports no result of its funnel plots (AMSTAR 2 low confidence on card sc_cortese_2018). The blood-pressure review is of high AMSTAR 2 confidence, but 87 of its 102 trials were industry funded and its risk of bias enters only its certainty ratings. The head-to-head trial is at some concerns (RoB 2: randomization and missing-data handling not described, blind not checked, parent ratings on a scale without norms). One level, not two: the trials were double-blind and the reviews used unpublished data.

inconsistency.note: No significant global inconsistency for the primary outcomes of the first review (common heterogeneity SD 0.188 and 0.178 for clinician ratings, 0.268 and 0.282 for leaving because of side effects). In the blood-pressure review heterogeneity was low or low to moderate in children and adolescents and moderate or moderate to high in adults, with local incoherence in 2 of 12 comparisons for each blood pressure and 4 of 10 for pulse in children and adolescents; the comparisons the statement uses were not significant either way.

indirectness.note: The comparison between the two medicines rests largely on indirect comparison through placebo, and in adults entirely so (no trial comparing them in either network); 'amphetamines' pools several products (lisdexamfetamine included in the first review), while the head-to-head trial tested dexamphetamine at one fixed dose of each drug in children for two weeks; trials were short (median 7 weeks; analyses at about 12 weeks) at licensed or guideline doses. The statement is worded for short-term prescribed use in people with ADHD.

imprecision.note: The symptom intervals exclude no difference (−0.44 to −0.05; −0.54 to −0.05), though they reach small values; the children's blood-pressure intervals are narrow (systolic −2.33 to 0.44 mm Hg). The intervals for leaving because of side effects are wide (0.94 to 2.73; 0.54 to 3.43), and the statement says a difference is neither shown nor ruled out rather than calling the two equal; that comparison alone would be rated down for imprecision.

publication_bias.note: The blood-pressure review's contour-enhanced funnel plots did not indicate small-study effects; the first review's funnel plots are only in its appendix (counted under risk of bias). Both reviews sought unpublished data from manufacturers and regulators (83% of trials in the first review).

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1; inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0. Low for the statement as worded: in short trials of prescribed medicines in people with ADHD, amphetamines gave a slightly larger reduction in clinician-rated symptoms than methylphenidate (the review's own GRADE: low in both age groups), while stopping because of side effects and rises in blood pressure and pulse were not shown to differ. Taken alone, the adult comparisons and the comparison of stopping would be very low (indirect only, or imprecise; the review rates the adult comparison of stopping very low), and the head-to-head trial's severity finding, one trial at one fixed dose of each drug with parent ratings on a scale without norms, would be low. Relation 'is associated with': the trials were randomized, but the comparison between the two drugs is mostly indirect, which is not a randomized comparison. Status single study: each finding rests on one source (symptoms and stopping on one network meta-analysis; blood pressure and pulse on a second that reused its searches and shares three authors; side-effect severity on one trial), and the trial-by-trial results are in appendices that were not read, so the trials inside the networks are not counted as independent replications here. Not rated: long-term effects, numbers of people who stop, psychosis (a separate answer) and use without a prescription.

statement: In 13- to 25-year-olds with ADHD in two US commercial insurance claims databases who started a prescribed stimulant between 2004 and 2015, starting amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine) compared with starting methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate) was associated with a higher rate of a new psychotic episode treated with an antipsychotic, although such episodes were rare after either: among 221,846 people matched one to one on a propensity score (110,923 in each group), 343 had an episode over a median follow-up of 113 to 162 days by group and database (about 4 to 5 months), about 1 in 650 (343 of 221,846 is 1 in 647, editors' calculation; the paper says approximately 1 in 660); 106 episodes followed methylphenidate and 237 amphetamine, 1.78 against 2.83 episodes per 1,000 person-years of use, a hazard ratio of 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09), prespecified as the primary analysis, and a difference of about 1 episode per 1,000 person-years (1.05, editors' calculation) (Moran et al., 2019). The paper's closing sentence, that the risk was about twice as high with amphetamine, rests on the crude shares of patients (0.21% against 0.10%), which do not allow for the longer time people who started amphetamine stayed in the study (median 155 against 113 days in one database and 162 against 123 in the other; from the printed counts and rates, about 83,700 against 59,600 person-years, editors' calculation): the two rates give a ratio of 1.59 (editors' calculation), and the hazard ratio is 1.65. The comparison is not randomized. People were matched on what the claims record (age, year, sex, region, insurance, markers of ADHD severity, other psychiatric diagnoses and medicines, recorded substance use disorders, type of prescriber and use of care; largest standardized difference 0.02); in the full unmatched cohort of 337,919 the hazard ratio was 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77) unadjusted and 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92) adjusted; two stricter definitions of psychosis gave 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) and 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22); emergency or inpatient care for alcohol, cannabis, opioid or other substance use disorders and for depression without psychosis, used as checks, did not differ between the groups (hazard ratios 0.91 to 1.12, all intervals including 1); and, by the authors' bias analysis, cannabis use would have had to be 97.0% among amphetamine starters, against an estimated 35.8% among people with ADHD, to explain the finding (assuming that any cannabis use doubles the risk of psychosis). Claims cannot show unrecorded drug use, early symptoms before psychosis, family history, the dose, or whether the medicines were taken; amphetamine was prescribed more to older patients and by family or internal medicine doctors (72.5% of their patients, against 51.6% of paediatricians'); and people who switched to the other stimulant (13.8% of methylphenidate starters, 5.6% of amphetamine starters) stopped being followed at the switch. Episodes in the first 7 days were not counted, and the median time to an episode was 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Psychosis counted only when coded and treated with an antipsychotic within 60 days (positive predictive value 91.3% in a review of records by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug, 93.1% in an outside validation), so milder or untreated symptoms are not counted. Results by age, by type of prescriber and by formulation were post hoc, with no test of whether subgroups differ. The people studied had commercial insurance; the authors say the results do not apply to people with public or no insurance, and the study says nothing about adults over 25, children under 13, use over years or use without a prescription. No other study on file measured psychosis with these medicines; the two network meta-analyses of trials did not study it. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Is psychosis more likely on amphetamine (as in Adderall) than on methylphenidate (as in Ritalin)? In one large US study of insurance records, a new psychotic episode treated with antipsychotic medicine was rare after starting either medicine, but somewhat more common after amphetamine. Among about 222,000 young people aged 13 to 25 with ADHD, matched on what their records showed, 343 had such an episode while followed for about 4 to 5 months, about 1 in 650. For every 1,000 people taking the medicine for a year, that was about 1.8 on methylphenidate and 2.8 on amphetamine: about 1.65 times the rate, or about 1 extra episode per 1,000 people a year. The authors' own summary, about twice as high, does not allow for amphetamine starters being followed for longer. The finding held with stricter definitions of psychosis, and emergency or hospital care for alcohol or cannabis use disorders was not more common after amphetamine. But it is not a trial: the records cannot show drug use that was never recorded, early signs of illness, the dose, or whether the pills were taken, and the study says nothing about longer use, adults over 25, or use without a prescription.
population: 337,919 people aged 13 to 25 with an outpatient ADHD diagnosis in two US commercial insurance claims databases (Optum Clinformatics, IBM MarketScan) who newly started a prescribed stimulant between January 2004 and September 2015, without earlier psychosis, bipolar disorder or antipsychotic use; 221,846 after 1:1 propensity-score matching (mean age about 17; about 37% female)
exposure: Starting amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine), as dispensed by an outpatient pharmacy; follow-up from day 7 after the first dispensing to 60 days after the end of supply, a switch to the other stimulant, psychosis or the end of data (dose not recorded)
comparator: Starting methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate), matched 1:1 on a propensity score within each database
outcome: A new psychotic episode: a new diagnosis code for psychosis with an antipsychotic prescription the same day or within 60 days (validated against records reviewed by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug), as incidence per 1,000 person-years and hazard ratio
magnitude: Moran et al. (2019). Matched population (primary, prespecified): 221,846 people (110,923 per group), 143,286 person-years; 343 episodes (2.4 per 1000 person-years); methylphenidate 106 (0.10%), amphetamine 237 (0.21%); incidence 1.78 against 2.83 per 1000 person-years; pooled hazard ratio 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09). Editors' calculations: 343 of 221,846 = 1 in 647 (paper: approximately 1 in 660); rate ratio 2.83/1.78 = 1.59; rate difference 1.05 per 1000 person-years (paper: approximately 1); person-years implied by the printed counts and rates 106/1.78 = about 59,600 and 237/2.83 = about 83,700 (sum about 143,300; printed 143,286); crude ratio from the counts 237/106 = 2.2. Median follow-up: Optum 155 (IQR 82 to 318) against 113 (82 to 209) days; MarketScan 162 (82 to 339) against 123 (82 to 228). Median time to the episode 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Full cohort (337,919: 119,708 and 218,211): 120 (0.10%) against 429 (0.20%); unadjusted HR 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77); adjusted 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92). Stricter definitions (matched): 89 (0.08%) against 211 (0.19%), HR 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), PPV 96.7%; 71 (0.06%) against 163 (0.15%), HR 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22), PPV 98.2%. Post hoc: 13 to 17 years 1.62 (1.24 to 2.12); 18 to 25 years 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00); family or internal medicine 1.78 (1.21 to 2.62); paediatricians 1.70 (1.09 to 2.67); psychiatrists 1.38 (0.93 to 2.04); extended-release only 1.77 (1.30 to 2.40); lisdexamfetamine against extended-release methylphenidate 1.54 (1.10 to 2.16); immediate-release 1.32 (0.77 to 2.29). Negative controls at 100 days: alcohol use disorder 1.12 (0.95 to 1.33), other substance use disorders 1.10 (0.95 to 1.29), cannabis 1.12 (0.91 to 1.38), opioids 0.91 (0.63 to 1.33), depression without psychotic features 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27). Bias analysis: cannabis use among amphetamine starters would need to be 97.0% (against 35.8%, relative risk 2.0 assumed). Switching: 16,489 of 119,708 (13.8%) and 12,233 of 218,211 (5.6%).

evidence.extracted: Cohort study in two US commercial insurance claims databases (Optum Clinformatics, IBM MarketScan) of people aged 13 to 25 with an outpatient ADHD diagnosis who newly started methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate) or amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine) between 1 January 2004 and 30 September 2015, with no prescription for either in the previous year; prior psychosis, bipolar disorder, CNS disease, antipsychotic or mood-stabilizer use and recent oral glucocorticoids excluded. Follow-up began 7 days after the first dispensing and stopped at psychosis, 60 days after the end of supply, a switch to the other stimulant, death, end of enrolment or 31 December 2016. Outcome: a new diagnosis code for psychosis with an antipsychotic prescription the same day or within 60 days (positive predictive value 93.1% in an outside health-record validation; 91.3% in a review of claims profiles by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug, with 10.1% and 8.4% of cases judged unlikely to be true psychosis). Primary analysis: 1:1 propensity-score matching within each database on all prespecified covariates (year, age, sex, region, insurance, markers of ADHD severity, other psychiatric disorders and medicines, substance use disorders, prescriber type, use of care), Cox models, pooled by fixed-effect meta-analysis; at least 80% power for a 50% higher risk.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: commercially insured US 13- to 25-year-olds starting prescribed stimulants for ADHD, the first months of use, psychosis treated with an antipsychotic; the statement says it does not cover public insurance, other ages, longer use, dose or use without a prescription.

imprecision.note: 343 events; the hazard ratio's interval (1.31 to 2.09) excludes no difference; the absolute rates are given.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; no registration is reported, but the primary analysis was prespecified before unblinding of exposure status and unadjusted, adjusted and matched estimates are all printed.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a claims cohort) starts low (METHODS §6.3); no domain downgraded and no upgrade (hazard ratio below 2; no dose data). The paper's closing description of the risk as about twice as high is not used: it rests on crude shares inflated by longer follow-up after amphetamine. Status single study: no replication is among the papers on file, and the two network meta-analyses of trials read in this round did not study psychosis.
